title: The house with four doors
hook: Guru Arjan builds the Harmandir Sahib low in the pool with doors on four sides, open to all

segments.voice: Yesterday, a jealous brother, Prithi Chand, and a Guru who answered with work, not revenge. Your line was pray for the difficult one. Did you wish them well, even once? Day sixty.

Think about how important buildings are usually designed. They sit up high, on a hill or on a platform. There's a grand staircase going up. There's one main entrance, maybe with a guard. The meaning is clear: this place is above you, and you come in by permission, through the front. Now picture the pool at Amritsar, the one Guru Ram Das began. His son, Guru Arjan, finished it, and then he did something unexpected. In the middle of the water, he began to build a house of God. And almost every choice he made about that building turns the usual meaning upside down. Today, the house in the middle of the pool.
screen: `HIGH UP, ONE GRAND ENTRANCE.` → `THE POOL AT AMRITSAR.` → `A HOUSE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WATER.`

segments.voice: It's called the Harmandir Sahib. Hari is a name for God, mandir means temple or house, and Sahib is a word of respect. The house of God. Many people know it as the Golden Temple, because of the gold that covers it; that came much later, in the nineteenth century. Here's what Guru Arjan did. First, instead of raising it high, he set it low. You walk down steps to reach it, so everyone who enters, rich or poor, comes down a little. Humility is built into the architecture. Second, instead of one grand entrance, he gave it doors on all four sides. In a world where people were sorted by caste and by creed, this house was open from every direction, to everyone. North, south, east, west. Remember Guru Nanak's feet toward the Kaaba, and the question: which way is God not? Here's that question turned into a building. And tradition adds one more detail. Many Sikhs say that the foundation stone was laid by a Muslim Sufi, Mian Mir, a friend of the Guru's from Lahore. Historians debate that story, but it has been told for a very long time, and it fits the house. The building was finished around 1604. It stands in the middle of the pool, reached by a causeway, and to this day the langar there feeds tens of thousands of people every day, of every faith and none. The house with four doors is still open on every side. What Guru Arjan placed at its center is the story of the next few days.
screen: `HARMANDIR — THE HOUSE OF GOD.` · `SET LOW: YOU WALK DOWN TO ENTER.` · `FOUR DOORS, FOR EVERY DIRECTION.` · `A FOUNDATION STONE, TRADITION SAYS.` · then, large: `OPEN ON EVERY SIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a door and leave it open. Settle first. Then, if you can, get up and open a door: your front door, a window, the door to your room. Stand in it for a moment. Feel the air come through. Think of who you'd welcome through it, and who you might have kept out without meaning to. Leave it open, for a while, if it's safe. The bell holds the time.
Harmandir Sahib. The house of God at Amritsar, set low in the pool with doors on four sides, open to all. Today's word.
Your line: open on every side. Today, open one door you've kept shut: a conversation, an invitation, a seat at your table. Day sixty.

howItsDone: The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is the holiest gurdwara for Sikhs; visitors of every faith cover their heads, walk down into the complex, circle the pool, and eat together in its langar, which serves people day and night.

fork.setup: you're Guru Arjan, building a house of God in the middle of a pool. how many doors does it get?
options: no doors: only priests may enter.
fork.reveal: Guru Arjan gave it four doors, one on each side, so it was open from every direction, to everyone.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Harmandir Sahib, hari, God, and mandir, house or temple; also called Darbar Sahib, the Golden Temple.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Golden Temple, a beautiful landmark.
what it means: a house of God set low, so all come down to enter, with doors on every side, open to all.
what a scholar hears: begun around 1588, finished around 1604; the gilding came under Maharaja Ranjit Singh; Mian Mir laying the foundation stone is tradition that historians debate.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition (the building of the Harmandir Sahib; Mian Mir and the foundation stone)

notes: Dates: construction begun about 1588 (some say 1589), completed about 1604. Confirm.
Mian Mir laying the foundation stone: late tradition; many historians doubt it. Framed as 'many Sikhs say' and 'historians debate'. Confirm.
Gilding under Maharaja Ranjit Singh in the early nineteenth century: confirm.
Langar numbers ('tens of thousands every day'; often cited as 50,000–100,000): confirm before release.
Hari etymology: 'Harmandir' is often explained as 'Hari's temple'; confirm.
The installation of the Adi Granth (day 62) is not taught here; the close points at the next few days.
